title: How to Use AR Try-On to Visualize Fashion and Jewelry Online
excerpt: Learn how to bring a fashion or jewelry image into the iDesignIts Design Studio, refine it, and preview it with a photo or webcam using AR Try-On.
content: Shopping for fashion and jewelry online is exciting-but sometimes you want to see how an item actually looks before deciding whether it is right for you.
With AR Try-On on iDesignIts, you can bring a fashion or jewelry image into the Design Studio, make adjustments if needed, and preview the design using a photo or your webcam.
Here's how it works.
1. Find an Image of the Item You Want to Try. Start by finding an image of the fashion or jewelry item you want to visualize.
You can use an image from your computer or phone, a website, an online fashion or jewelry store, your own design, or an image you have created or downloaded.
For example, you might find an image of a necklace, earring, dress, top, or another fashion accessory that you would like to preview.
Tip: Choose an image where the item is clearly visible. A clean image with good contrast can make it easier to work with.
2. Open the iDesignIts Design Studio. Go to iDesignIts and open the Design Studio.
Once you are inside the studio, look at the menu on the left side.
Find the S - Source button.
Clicking S - Source opens the source window where you can bring your chosen image into the Design Studio.
3. Upload Your Image. Upload the image you found or created.
Once the image is loaded into the Design Studio, you can work with it before trying it on.
This is particularly useful when the original image needs some adjustments.
4. Modify the Design if Needed. Depending on what you are creating, you can modify the image or design before using AR Try-On.
You might want to adjust the shape, change the size, edit the design, remove unwanted portions, change colors, refine the artwork, or experiment with different variations.
This gives designers more flexibility to experiment before visualizing the final design.
5. Select the Type of Item. Next, select the type of article you want to try on.
Depending on the available options, this can include items such as Garment, Necklace, Earring, Accessory, and other supported fashion items.
Selecting the appropriate article type helps the try-on experience understand what you are trying to visualize.
6. Choose How You Want to Try It On. Now it's time for the fun part.
Choose whether you want to use a photo or your webcam.
Try Using a Photo. Choose the photo option if you already have a picture you want to use.
Upload your photo and let the AR Try-On experience visualize the selected item on the image.
This is convenient when you don't want to use your camera or when you already have a suitable photo.
Try Using Your Webcam. Prefer a live preview? Choose the webcam option.
Allow camera access when prompted, and the AR Try-On experience can use your camera to provide a live visualization.
This lets you move naturally and see how the selected design appears as you interact with the experience.
7. See Your Design in AR. Once everything is selected, try on your design.
The AR experience brings together your selected fashion or jewelry item and your photo or live camera view, giving you a way to visualize the design before making a decision.
For shoppers, this can make online browsing more interactive.
For designers, it provides another way to evaluate a concept and see how a design works in a more realistic context.
Why Use AR Try-On? Traditional online shopping usually gives you product photos and descriptions. AR Try-On adds another layer of visualization.

It can help you explore a design before purchasing, compare different styles, visualize jewelry or fashion accessories, experiment with your own designs, get a better sense of how an item appears when worn, and make the online shopping experience more interactive.
From Inspiration to Try-On. One of the useful things about the iDesignIts workflow is that you don't have to start with a finished design.
You can find an image, bring it into the Design Studio using the S - Source button, modify it if necessary, select the appropriate article type, and then use AR Try-On with a photo or webcam.
Find an image -> Upload -> Modify -> Select article type -> Try using Photo or Webcam -> Try On.
That makes the process useful not only for shoppers, but also for designers who want to experiment with ideas and visualize their creations.
Start Exploring. Fashion design doesn't have to stop at a picture on a screen.
With digital editing and AR Try-On, you can move from inspiration to design to visualization in one creative workflow.
Explore your ideas with iDesignIts Design Studio and see where your next design takes you.
A quick note: When downloading images from websites, make sure you have permission to use them and respect the image owner's copyright and any applicable usage terms.

title: How to Upload an Image to the iDesignIts Design Studio
excerpt: Learn the three main ways to prepare an uploaded fashion or jewelry image in the iDesignIts Design Studio, from automatic trace to AI background removal and manual cutting.
content: Want to turn an image of a fashion or jewelry item into something you can work with in the iDesignIts Design Studio?

The Design Studio provides several ways to prepare an uploaded image. In most cases, the website can automatically trace the article for you. If that doesn't work, you have additional options-including an AI background remover and a manual cutting tool.
Here's how to do it.
1. Upload Your Image and Let the Website Trace It. Start by uploading the image of the article you want to use.
Once the image is uploaded, iDesignIts will attempt to trace the article automatically.
The tracing process identifies the main article in the image so that it can be separated from the surrounding background and used in the Design Studio.
If the article is traced successfully, review the result.
If you're happy with it, click Add to Canvas.
Your article will then be added to the canvas, where you can continue editing or designing.
Quick workflow: Upload Image -> Automatic Trace -> Review -> Add to Canvas.
This is the easiest option and should be your first choice.
2. If Automatic Tracing Doesn't Work, Try AI Background Remover. Sometimes an image can be difficult to trace.
For example, the background might be complicated, the article might blend into the background, or the image may not have enough contrast between the subject and its surroundings.
If the automatic tracing doesn't give you a good result, try the AI Background Remover.
The AI Background Remover can help separate the main article from its background.
After the background has been removed, review the result and, if it looks good, add the article to your canvas.
Second option: Upload Image -> AI Background Remover -> Review -> Add to Canvas.
This gives you another way to prepare the image without having to manually cut it out.
3. If Both Options Fail, Add the Original Image. Not every image is easy for automated tools to process.
If both automatic tracing and the AI Background Remover don't produce the result you want, you can still use the original image.
Choose Add Original Image.
This places the complete original image onto the canvas.
You can then manually select the part of the image you actually want to use.
4. Use the Scissors Tool to Cut Out the Article. Once the original image is on the canvas, look at the menu on the left side of the Design Studio.
Select the Scissors tool.
Use the scissors to manually cut around the article you want to keep.
This option gives you direct control over the selection and can be especially useful when automatic tools have difficulty identifying the article.
For example, if you have a photograph containing a necklace against a complicated background, you can manually cut around the necklace and remove the portions you don't need.
Manual workflow: Add Original Image -> Select Scissors -> Cut Around Article -> Keep the Desired Article.
Three Ways to Prepare Your Image. The iDesignIts Design Studio gives you a simple fallback process.
Option 1 - Automatic Trace. Upload the image and let the website trace the article. If successful -> Add to Canvas.
Option 2 - AI Background Remover. If automatic tracing doesn't work well, try the AI Background Remover. If successful -> Add to Canvas.

Option 3 - Manual Scissors Tool. If neither automated method gives you a good result, add the original image and manually cut out the article using the Scissors tool. Add Original Image -> Scissors -> Cut -> Design.
Which Method Should You Use? Start with the simplest option and move to the next one only when necessary.
Automatic Trace is the fastest approach when the article is clearly visible.
AI Background Remover is a useful alternative when the background makes automatic tracing difficult.
Scissors gives you the most direct control when you need to manually decide exactly which part of the image should become your design.
This three-step approach means that even when an image isn't easy for automated processing, you still have a way to bring the article into your canvas.
Start Designing. Once your article has been successfully added to the canvas, you're ready to continue designing.
You can experiment with the design, make adjustments, and eventually use the article with other iDesignIts features such as AR Try-On.
Upload -> Trace -> Remove Background -> Cut Manually -> Add to Canvas -> Design.
The goal is to make it easy to take an image you already have and turn it into something you can creatively work with inside the iDesignIts Design Studio.
Tip: For the best results, start with a clear image where the article is easy to distinguish from its background. And remember to use images you have permission to edit and reuse.

title: How to Create and Shape Dot Art in the iDesignIts Design Studio
excerpt: Learn how to turn dots on, drag and group them, and reshape them into fashion concepts, jewelry ideas, decorative patterns, and custom silhouettes inside the Design Studio.
content: Looking for a simple and creative way to experiment with shapes? Dot Art in the iDesignIts Design Studio lets you transform a collection of dots into almost any shape you can imagine.
Whether you're creating a fashion concept, jewelry design, decorative artwork, or simply experimenting with digital shapes, Dot Art gives you a flexible way to build and reshape your ideas.
1. Turn On the Dots. Open the iDesignIts Design Studio and find the Dot button.
Click the Dot button once.
A collection of dots will appear on the canvas.
These dots can now be moved and reshaped to create your own design.
2. Turn the Dots Off. Finished working with the dots or want to see your design without them?
Simply click the Dot button again.
The dots will be turned off.
You can click the button again whenever you want to bring them back.
3. Drag the Dots to Create Your Shape. This is where the creative part begins.
You can drag individual dots around the canvas to reshape the arrangement.
Move the dots closer together, spread them apart, or reposition them to create the outline you want.
With enough experimentation, you can transform the original arrangement into many different forms.
For example, you can create curves, letters, symbols, jewelry-inspired shapes, decorative patterns, abstract designs, and custom silhouettes.
Think of each dot as a small building block. Move enough of them around and you can gradually transform the entire design.
4. Move a Group of Dots Together. You don't always need to move the dots one at a time.
If you want to move several dots together, right-click on the canvas and select Group Dots.
Once the dots are grouped, you can drag the group and move them together.
This is especially useful when you have already created part of a design and want to reposition it without disturbing the arrangement of the individual dots.
Group workflow: Right-click -> Group Dots -> Select the Group -> Drag.
Grouping can save time when working with larger or more detailed dot designs.
5. Create Your Own Dot Art. The fun part of Dot Art is that there isn't just one correct shape.
Start with the dots and experiment.
Move individual dots to refine the shape. Group dots when you want to reposition a larger section. Turn the dots off when you want to view your work without the dot overlay.
You can gradually turn a simple collection of points into a completely different design.
Quick Guide. Show dots: Click Dot. Hide dots: Click Dot again. Reshape: Drag individual dots. Move multiple dots: Right-click -> Group Dots -> Drag. Experiment: Move, group, reshape, and refine.
Turn Dots Into Ideas. Dot Art is a simple tool, but it can become surprisingly powerful when you start experimenting.
Click the Dot button. Move the dots. Shape your idea. Group them when needed.
With iDesignIts, your design doesn't have to begin as a perfect shape-it can start with a collection of dots and evolve into whatever you imagine.

title: Pen and Ghost Tools in iDesignIts: Create Lines, Meshes, and Flexible Design Patterns
excerpt: Learn the difference between Pen and Ghost lines, how to build visible linework or temporary structure, and how to combine them with Dot Art for flexible design patterns.
content: The Pen and Ghost tools in the iDesignIts Design Studio give you different ways to add lines and structure to your designs.
Both tools can be used to create interesting patterns, outlines, and mesh-like designs-but there is one important difference.
Pen lines are always visible. Ghost lines are visible only when the dots are visible or selected.
This makes the two tools useful for different stages of the design process.
The Pen Tool. The Pen tool creates lines that remain visible on your design.
Select the Pen tool from the left-side menu and draw your line on the canvas.
Once created, the line remains visible even when the dots are turned off.
Draw a Single Line. You can use the Pen tool to create a simple single line.
This can be useful for outlines, decorative elements, design details, connecting points, and creating custom shapes.
Simply draw the line where you want it on the canvas.
Create Multiple Lines. The Pen tool isn't limited to a single line.
You can create multiple lines to build more complex designs.
Multiple lines can be arranged together to create patterns, structured shapes, or decorative elements.
This is particularly useful when you're building a design that requires repeated lines or a more detailed visual structure.
Create a Mesh. You can also use the Pen tool to create a mesh.
A mesh is made from multiple lines arranged together, creating a structured network or grid-like appearance.
Meshes can be useful for creating decorative patterns, fashion design elements, jewelry concepts, geometric artwork, and structured shapes.
The spacing between the lines in the mesh can be adjusted, giving you control over how dense or open the design appears.
Adjusting Mesh Spacing. Want a tighter mesh? Reduce the spacing between the lines.
Want a more open design? Increase the spacing.
This allows you to experiment with different levels of detail without having to completely redraw your design.
The Ghost Tool. The Ghost tool works differently from Pen.
Ghost lines are designed to be visible only when the dots are visible or selected.
This makes Ghost particularly useful when you want to work with the underlying dot structure without having permanent lines displayed on your final design.
For example, you might use Ghost lines while shaping a design with Dot Art.
When the dots are visible, the Ghost lines help you see the connections and structure.
When the dots are turned off, the Ghost lines disappear.
Pen vs. Ghost. The easiest way to remember the difference is this: Pen lines stay visible when dots are hidden. Ghost lines do not.
Pen: Draw -> Line stays visible.
Ghost: Draw -> Line appears with dots -> Line disappears when dots are hidden.
Combine Pen, Ghost, and Dot Art. The real flexibility comes from using these tools together.
You can start with Dot Art, move the dots into the shape you want, and then use Ghost lines to work with the dot structure.
Once you're happy with the design, use Pen to create permanent lines that remain visible.
You can then build multiple lines or a mesh and adjust the spacing to achieve the look you're after.
A simple workflow: Dots -> Shape -> Ghost -> Refine -> Pen -> Create Lines or Mesh -> Adjust Spacing.
This gives you both a flexible working structure and permanent design elements.
Experiment With Your Design. Pen and Ghost give you two different ways to approach line-based design.
Use Ghost when you want lines that work alongside your dots and disappear when the dots are hidden.
Use Pen when you want your lines to remain part of the visible design.
Whether you're creating a simple line, multiple lines, or a detailed mesh, you can adjust the spacing and arrangement to create the effect you want.
Start with dots, experiment with Ghost, and turn your finished ideas into permanent designs with Pen.

title: Colors and Fabric: Customize Your Designs in iDesignIts
excerpt: Learn how to use the color picker, jewelry material presets, and fabric copy tools to explore different finishes, patterns, and variations in the iDesignIts Design Studio.
content: Color and fabric can completely change the character of a fashion or jewelry design. The iDesignIts Design Studio gives you several ways to experiment with both, from choosing a custom color to applying realistic-looking materials and copying fabric from one design to another.
Whether you're working on a garment, jewelry concept, or creative fashion design, these tools make it easier to explore different possibilities.
1. Choose a Color With the Color Picker. The easiest way to select a color is to use the Color Picker.
Choose the color you want and apply it to your design.
You can experiment with different shades and combinations to see how your design changes.
This is especially useful when you already have a specific color in mind or want to create your own custom color.
2. Choose From Jewelry Colors. For jewelry designs, iDesignIts also provides ready-to-use material colors.
You can choose from options such as Gold, Silver, Bronze, Platinum, and Rose Gold.
These presets make it easy to quickly explore different metal finishes without having to manually select a color each time.
For example, you can take the same necklace design and experiment with gold, silver, platinum, or rose gold to see which finish works best.
3. Choose Fabric With the Color Picker. The Color Picker isn't limited to solid colors.
You can also use it when working with fabric.
Select the area or color you want to work with and experiment with different fabric colors to create the appearance you're looking for.
This gives you the flexibility to customize a garment without having to start the design from scratch.
4. Copy Fabric From One Image to Another. One of the more useful features is the ability to copy a fabric patch from one image and apply it to another.
This can be helpful when you find a fabric texture or pattern that you want to use on a different design.
Here's how.
Step 1: Lock the Image. First, click the Lock button.
Locking the image prevents it from moving while you select the fabric.
This makes it easier to work precisely with a particular section of the image.
Step 2: Select a Patch of Fabric. Once the image is locked, select the patch of fabric you want to copy.
Choose an area that represents the fabric or pattern you want to transfer to another design.
Step 3: Right-Click and Copy Fabric. Right-click on the selected fabric patch.
Choose Copy Fabric.
The selected fabric is now ready to be used elsewhere.
Step 4: Move to the Other Image. Open or select the image where you want to apply the fabric.
Position yourself over the area where you want the copied fabric to appear.
Step 5: Paste Fabric. Right-click and choose Paste Fabric.
The copied fabric can now be applied to the new design.
The complete workflow: Lock Image -> Select Fabric Patch -> Right-click -> Copy Fabric -> Select Another Image -> Right-click -> Paste Fabric.
Why Copy Fabric? Copying fabric makes it easier to experiment with different design combinations.
For example, you might find a beautiful fabric pattern in one garment image and want to explore how that same fabric could look on another design.
Instead of recreating the fabric manually, you can copy a patch and use it in another image.
This can be particularly useful for fashion concepts, garment variations, pattern experimentation, fabric comparisons, design inspiration, and creating different versions of the same design.
Explore Different Materials and Colors. A single design can look completely different when you change its color, metal finish, or fabric.
Try experimenting with Color Picker -> Gold -> Silver -> Bronze -> Platinum -> Rose Gold -> Fabric -> Copy Fabric -> Paste Fabric.
The more you experiment, the easier it becomes to discover combinations you might not have considered initially.
Design Without Starting Over. Colors and fabrics don't have to be permanent decisions.
With the iDesignIts Design Studio, you can experiment with different colors and materials, copy fabric between images, and explore variations of your design.
Pick a color. Try a material. Copy a fabric. Create another variation.
Your original idea can become the starting point for many new designs.

title: How to Design Custom Jewelry for AR Try-Ons
excerpt: Learn a practical workflow for turning jewelry concepts into browser-based AR try-on experiences without sacrificing fit, finish, or visual clarity.
content: Designing jewelry for AR try-ons is different from designing a static catalog render. Every shape, clasp, connector, and highlight has to stay readable when it is placed over a moving body in a live camera feed.

Start with a simplified silhouette. Thin chains and tiny decorative details often disappear in browser-based previews, so the first goal is not realism. The first goal is legibility. Build a clean outline, then layer in texture and material cues only after the base form reads at arm's length.

The next step is placement logic. Necklaces, pendants, and collar pieces need a stable visual center of gravity. If the design is asymmetrical, test it against different shoulder angles and torso movement to make sure the composition still looks intentional during motion.

Color and material testing should also happen early. Highly reflective metallic gradients can look elegant in a static graphic but blow out under webcam compression. A better approach is to test gold, silver, platinum, and gemstone palettes against both warm and cool skin tones in moderate indoor lighting.

Finally, package the design for iteration. Save versions with different scales, simplified pendant geometry, and alternate clasp spacing. The strongest AR-ready jewelry designs are usually the ones that have been edited down until their most distinctive features survive motion, lighting changes, and small-screen previews.

title: Step-by-Step Clothing Design Frameworks for Beginners
excerpt: A beginner-friendly process for moving from inspiration to structure, silhouette, fabric direction, and presentation inside a browser-based design workflow.
content: Beginners often jump straight into decoration before the garment shape is doing any work. That usually leads to noisy designs that feel unfinished. A better framework is to decide the silhouette first, then define seams, then test proportion, and only then add material and embellishment.

Start with one clear garment idea. It may be a fitted top, a draped dress, a structured jacket, or an exaggerated sleeve concept. Translate that idea into a simple body-facing outline with obvious front-view proportions. The early draft should answer one question clearly: what kind of garment is this meant to be?

Once the silhouette is stable, divide the garment into functional zones. Identify neckline, waist shaping, hem direction, sleeve behavior, and panel transitions. Thinking in zones keeps the design readable and makes later changes more deliberate.

After structure comes surface. Test fills, swatches, line weight, and trim only after the design already works in plain form. This is the easiest way to avoid depending on decoration to rescue weak proportions.

The last step is presentation. Export versions that show the flat design, a close-up material pass, and a try-on or mannequin preview. Good clothing design communication depends on clarity, not just style, and beginners improve much faster when every design pass is documented in a repeatable sequence.

title: A Complete Guide to Vector Editing for Fashion
excerpt: Understand how vector paths, control points, fills, scaling, and layering support cleaner apparel and accessory concepts in digital workflows.
content: Vector editing is useful in fashion because it preserves edge clarity. When you scale a neckline, reshape a pendant outline, or refine a sleeve opening, the geometry stays editable instead of degrading into pixels.

The most important habit is learning to separate shape decisions from texture decisions. First adjust the anchor points and path flow until the silhouette is balanced. Only then should you apply fills, textures, repeated motifs, or decorative overlays.

Layering also matters. Keep base shapes, detail lines, trim, and embellishment on separate conceptual layers, even if the interface does not expose formal layer panels. This makes revisions faster and reduces accidental distortion when moving or resizing complex artwork.

For fashion work, point editing should follow visual tension. Curves around collars, armholes, and hems should feel intentional and smooth rather than mathematically even. A technically perfect path can still look wrong if it does not support the drape or structure of the garment.

The best vector workflow is iterative. Duplicate, test, compare, and remove unnecessary complexity. Clean vectors communicate professionalism because they preserve decisions clearly across sketches, fittings, mockups, and final presentation assets.
